analysis.one_liner: Made it much harder for people to erase credit card debt by bankruptcy, pushing them into repayment plans.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the House 306-108 and the Senate 82-16, and the House approved a final compromise 244-116 in November 2002, but the Senate never voted on that final version before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten consumer bankruptcy to apply an income formula — a 'means test' — that assumes anyone with income above their state's median can repay, and would have forced every filer to get paid credit counseling first. It shortened how often people could file, added paperwork that gets cases dismissed, and cut the property people could shield from creditors. It also carried real benefits for some people: child support moved to first priority and became impossible to erase, retirement and education savings were protected, and family farmers and fishermen got permanent bankruptcy relief. The House passed it in March 2001, the Senate passed its own version in July 2001, and after a year of closed-door negotiation the House approved the final compromise on November 15, 2002 — but the Senate never took it up before the Congress ended, so it died.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card issuers, banks, and other lenders, who would have collected more from people who today get a fresh start: the means test pushes higher-earning debtors into five-year court-supervised repayment plans instead of erasing unsecured debt. Family farmers and fishermen, who would have gotten permanent Chapter 12 relief, and people owed child support, who would have gotten first-priority status, also benefited.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a formula-based 'means test' that presumes abuse whenever a debtor's income exceeds their state median, pushing those debtors from Chapter 7 (debts erased) into Chapter 3 or 13 repayment plans that pay unsecured creditors like credit card companies [S3][S6].
Requires everyone filing bankruptcy to first complete a paid briefing from an approved credit counseling agency and a financial management course before any discharge [S3][S6].
Extends the waiting period between Chapter 7 discharges from six to eight years and speeds up dismissal of cases with incomplete paperwork [S5][S6].
Caps the homestead exemption wealthy debtors can claim at $125,000 and tightens the definition of protected household goods, closing shelters used by high-income filers [S5][S6].
Moves child support and alimony to first priority among claims, makes them harder to discharge, and lets collection continue during bankruptcy [S3][S5].
Protects tax-exempt retirement funds and education savings accounts from creditors, and adds credit card minimum-payment warnings and other Truth in Lending disclosures [S3][S5].
Permanently reenacts Chapter 12 for family farmers, raises their debt ceiling from $1.5 million to about $3.2 million, and extends the same chapter to family fishermen [S5][S6].

analysis.who_pays: People who file bankruptcy: they would pay for counseling and more attorney time, fill out heavier documentation, and many above the median income would be pushed into five-year repayment plans instead of getting a fresh start — with the burden falling on people hit by job loss, divorce, and medical bills.

drawbacks.text: The means test is a rigid formula: debtors above their state median income must repay under IRS-standard budgets, even when their actual circumstances — medical bills, temporary unemployment, local costs — don't fit the formula, and rebutting the presumption requires extensive documentation [S3][S6].
Mandatory pre-filing credit counseling adds a fee and a waiting period before someone in crisis can file at all, creating a paid gatekeeper between debtors and the court [S3][S6].

Heavier documentation duties and automatic dismissal for missing paperwork, plus attorney liability for filing a Chapter 7 that fails the test, would raise the cost of filing and push some people to go unrepresented [S3][S6].

The Senate version added untracked side provisions — increased home energy assistance funding and expanded federal energy-savings contracting — that had nothing to do with bankruptcy, illustrating how the bill became a vehicle for unrelated items [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine benefits — child support priority, retirement savings protection, permanent family farmer relief, and better credit disclosures — are real but small beside the main effect, which shifts power in bankruptcy from debtors to creditors. The means test, counseling mandate, and documentation burdens would have made relief slower, costlier, and harder for exactly the people the bankruptcy system exists to help, while the disclosure provisions are modest compensation.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed their own versions, negotiators produced a final compromise, and the House approved it 244-116 on November 15, 2002 — but the Senate never voted on it, and the bill died when the two-year Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 306-108 on March 1, 2001, after defeating a Democratic motion to recommit 165-253 [S10][S11][S9].
The Senate cut off debate on a motion to proceed 88-10 and passed its own amended version 82-16 on July 17, 2001, appointing conferees including Leahy, Biden, Hatch, and Grassley [S12][S13][S9].

The House agreed to conference on July 31, 2001, instructing conferees to keep the family farmer and fisherman protections; the conference committee met in May 2002 and filed its report in July 2002 [S9][S6].

A rule needed to bring up the conference report failed on November 14, 2002, but the House instead passed a motion to agree to the Senate amendment with an amendment by 244-116 on November 15 — 189 of 223 Republicans voting yes, 115 of 208 Democrats voting no [S14][S9].
The Senate received the House's final version the same day but took no further action, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2003, so the bill never became law [S9].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People facing bankruptcy kept the older, more flexible law, which lets judges consider their actual circumstances instead of a formula. Credit card issuers, who had sought this bill for years, did not get the collections boost it would have provided — though Congress passed a nearly identical bill a few years later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People facing bankruptcy, and consumer advocates

for.name: Rep. George Gekas
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-PA); bill sponsor and chairman of the Judiciary subcommittee on commercial and administrative law
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 31, 2001, and later moved to call up the final conference report in the House.

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee 19-8 and, after the Senate passed it, moved that the House disagree to the Senate amendment and agree to a conference, then served as a House conferee.

for.name: 212 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage on March 1, 2001 (Roll 25), with no voting Republican opposed; 189 of them voted yes again on the final version in November 2002.

for.name: 45 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed (88-10) and for final passage (82-16) in July 2001.

for.name: Credit card and consumer lending industry
for.role: Major campaign contributors and lobbying force, whose members had sought means-test legislation for years
for.what_they_did: Lobbied heavily for the bill over multiple Congresses; it was widely understood as the industry's top legislative priority.

against.name: Senate majority (Democrats held 49 of 100 seats)
against.role: Controlled the Senate floor schedule from June 2001 through the end of the Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House-passed final version to a vote after receiving it on November 15, 2002; the Congress ended with the bill sitting at the desk.

against.name: 115 of 208 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the motion to agree to the Senate amendment with an amendment on November 15, 2002 (Roll 484), after 107 of them voted no on original passage in March 2001.

against.name: Rep. John Conyers
against.what_they_did: Objected to voice votes on amendments in committee of the whole and moved to recommit the bill with instructions; the motion failed 165-253.

against.name: 14 of 49 Senate Democrats
against.role: Senate Democrats opposed to the bill
against.what_they_did: Voted against final Senate passage on July 17, 2001 (Roll 236).

against.name: Consumer, labor, and women's groups
against.role: National advocacy organizations concerned with debtor protections
against.what_they_did: Opposed the means test and counseling mandate as punishing people driven into debt by job loss, divorce, and medical bills.

sides.party_line_note: The bill passed with large bipartisan majorities in both chambers, but the parties pulled in opposite directions: on House passage, all 212 voting Republicans were in favor while House Democrats split 93-107 against, and on the final 2002 vote 189 of 223 Republicans voted yes against 55 of 208 Democrats; in the Senate, 36 of 50 Democrats and 45 of 49 Republicans voted yes.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and unsecured consumer lenders
industries.note: The means test, counseling requirement, and heavier paperwork would have pushed more debtors into full or partial repayment of credit card debt instead of erasing it, directly increasing collections. The bill died, so the industry kept operating under the older debtor-friendlier law. [S3][S6]

Mandatory pre-filing counseling would have made approved nonprofit agencies the gatekeeper every bankruptcy filer must pass through, typically for a fee, before the court would even accept the case. The requirement functions as a screen between debtors and relief. [S3][S6]

Title IX would have exempted their contracts from the automatic stay, allowed immediate setoffs, and protected netting arrangements when a counterparty fails, letting financial firms seize collateral faster than other creditors and leaving less for ordinary unsecured creditors. [S5][S6]

The bill permanently reenacted Chapter 12, raised the qualifying debt limit from $1.5 million to $3.237 million, and extended it to fishermen, letting family operations restructure rather than liquidate. This was the price of support that won votes in both parties. [S5][S6]

industries.industry: Wealthy debtors using state homestead shelters
industries.note: The bill capped the homestead exemption at $125,000 and tightened rules on moving to a state to shield assets, closing loopholes used by high-income filers while doing nothing comparable for ordinary filers. [S5][S6]
